evals.prompt: I run KestrelConf, a community-run Go and distributed-systems conference in Porto, volunteer organizers, third edition, 320 attendees expected. The event is on 12 March and we are four months out. Our CFP closed last week and we publish the full schedule on Monday, so we finally have something concrete to show companies. Last edition seven companies backed us. I need to raise EUR 38,000. Give me the plan for getting that money in.
evals.expected_output: A plan that opens by flagging the timing problem: sponsor outreach belongs around eight months out because budgets lock in the prior financial year, and waiting for the finished program inverted the correct order. It then salvages the remaining window by prioritizing prospects whose budget cycle is still open, sizes the list backward from the EUR 38,000 goal with rates flagged as self-set assumptions, splits the seven returning sponsors from net-new into two motions, and constrains what a community-run event can promise.
expectations: States that sponsor outreach should have begun roughly eight months before the event date, not four
Gives the reason as sponsor budgets, especially at larger companies, being locked in during the prior financial year
States that outreach is the first external-facing motion of the plan, ahead of the CFP and ahead of attendee marketing
Does not present the newly published schedule as the right trigger for starting sponsor outreach
Recommends prioritizing targets whose budget cycle is still open rather than pitching the full list uniformly
Advises asking each prospect which month their team plans next year's event budget, so the next edition starts from that record
Sizes the target list backward from the EUR 38,000 goal divided by an average package price, rather than proposing a fixed company count
Labels any close rate or reply rate used in that math as a self-set assumption rather than a published sponsorship benchmark
Splits the seven returning sponsors from net-new prospects and runs them as two distinct motions rather than one list
Produces a scored target list with a top-3-to-5 callout naming why each of those goes first
Rules out promising attendee lists or purchasable speaking slots, because the event sits on the community-run pole

evals.prompt: Draft the first email to Brannock Systems, a Berlin observability vendor we want as a sponsor for DeltaHack, our 500-person student hackathon on 8-10 April at Aveiro University. Nobody on our team knows anyone there. I found their Head of Developer Relations, Lena Mirov, on LinkedIn, and we want them mainly because they keep saying publicly they want feedback on their new tracing agent. I want to attach our 11-page sponsor prospectus PDF and drop our Calendly link in so she can just book a slot, plus our logo in the signature so it looks legit.
evals.expected_output: A first email stripped of every attachment, hyperlink and image, with the reason given, plus a specific curiosity-driving subject line, the event basics, a plain-language explanation of what a hackathon is, a Brannock-specific angle, one differentiator, and a concrete proposed call time. It also raises the referral ask as the stronger first touch where no warm path exists, and confirms Developer Relations as the right title for a product-feedback motivation.
expectations: Refuses to attach the sponsor prospectus PDF to the first email
Excludes every hyperlink and image from the first email, explicitly including the Calendly link and the signature logo
Gives corporate phishing and spam filtering auto-trashing the mail unread as the reason for that rule
States that the prospectus, the booking link and the website all wait for a follow-up message
Proposes a specific, curiosity-driving subject line rather than a flat 'DeltaHack and Brannock Systems partnership'-style label
The draft states the event size, location and dates: 500 participants, Aveiro University, 8-10 April
The draft explains in plain terms what a hackathon is, instead of assuming the recipient knows the format
The draft carries a Brannock-specific angle tied to the tracing agent feedback they have asked for publicly
The draft names one differentiator setting DeltaHack apart from other events soliciting the same company
The draft proposes a specific time for a call instead of asking the recipient to say what works
Raises the referral ask - one no-pitch message to someone senior to Lena Mirov asking only who owns sponsorship decisions - as a higher-yield first touch where no warm path exists
Confirms Developer Relations as the right title to target for a product-feedback motivation

evals.prompt: Our sponsor prospectus for NorthLoop Summit is finished: five tiers from EUR 1,500 to EUR 12,000, full benefits tables, properly designed by an actual designer. I have 15 target companies with named contacts pulled together this week. My plan is to blast the deck out on Tuesday with a short cover note, then chase whoever opens it and ignore the rest. Sanity check the plan before I hit send.
evals.expected_output: A rejection of the prospectus-first blast, replacing it with a warm-path check per target, an exploratory call before any document is sent, and a proposal sent the same day as that call with the single most relevant package highlighted, tied to the metric the sponsor named, and carrying a deadline. Open-tracking is replaced by pipeline-stage tracking.
expectations: Rejects sending the prospectus as the first touch
Places an exploratory call before the prospectus is sent
States the proposal goes out immediately after the call, same day, rather than as the opening move
Sends the prospectus with the single most relevant package highlighted, not as an undifferentiated five-tier deck
Requires the proposal to state why this package fits this specific sponsor, tied to the success metric the sponsor named on the call
Requires a sponsorship deadline attached to the proposal
Structures the call so the organizer pitches the event and team briefly and then lets the sponsor talk
Includes asking the sponsor what success metrics they used on past sponsorships and what they spent and got out of them
Qualifies authority, need, urgency and money during the call
Instructs scheduling the follow-up call before the first call ends
Requires a warm-path check per target - whether anyone on the organizing team or in the community works at or knows someone at each company - before any colder channel
Replaces chasing whoever opened the deck with tracking every one of the 15 prospects by pipeline stage

evals.prompt: Help me size the sponsor prospecting list for Fernweh Devfest. Revenue goal is EUR 60,000, our average package over the last two editions has been about EUR 5,000, and we are a two-person volunteer team with maybe four hours a week between us. How many companies do we need on the list, what conversion rates should I plan on, and how will I know halfway through whether we are on track?
evals.expected_output: Backward pipeline math from EUR 60,000 to 12 sponsors to prospects to a target-list size, with both rates explicitly marked as self-set assumptions rather than benchmarks, a 2-3x sourcing multiple on top, a capped follow-up cadence suited to two volunteers, and pipeline coverage plus stage conversion named as the mid-way checks.
expectations: Computes sponsors needed as the revenue goal divided by average package price, reaching 12 sponsors from EUR 60,000 and EUR 5,000
Divides sponsors needed by an assumed close rate to get prospects to pitch, then by an assumed reply rate to get target-list size
Explicitly labels both the close rate and the reply rate as self-set assumptions rather than established rates
States that event sponsorship publishes no close-rate or reply-rate benchmark of its own
Warns against planning on B2B SaaS figures such as 9-15% reply or 20-30% close as if they were sponsorship facts
Tells the team to write the assumed rates down as assumptions and replace them with their own observed edition-over-edition rates
Applies a 2-3x sourcing multiple on top of the computed list, because qualification culls hard
Names pipeline coverage - prospects in play versus the backward-sized list - as the mid-way on-track check, and notes a shortfall there predicts a shortfall at close months earlier
Names stage conversion across first touch to call, call to proposal, and proposal to close as the second measure, tracked per channel and per motion
Recommends the capped sponsor-standard follow-up cadence for a two-person volunteer team rather than a longer multi-angle sales sequence
Recommends diversifying the list across startups, midsized companies and large enterprises instead of concentrating on one segment

evals.prompt: Sent the proposal to Kettleridge Analytics 16 days ago after a genuinely good call. Total silence since. I have already pinged twice, on day 4 and day 10, both of them 'just circling back to see if you had a chance to look at this'. Kestrel Summit is on 27 November so we are five months out. What do I send next and how long do I keep going? Separate thing: another prospect replied yesterday with 'please take me off this list' but she is already queued into the same sequence for three more sends.
evals.expected_output: A next touch carrying a genuinely new angle instead of another bump, a cap of three follow-ups spaced one to two weeks apart, the 3-4 day tightening explicitly reserved for the run-up to the event, a final reminder anchored to a real production deadline already on the calendar, and the opted-out contact removed on the spot with the three queued sends cancelled.
expectations: Names the 'circling back' / 'just checking in' bump as a move to drop entirely rather than one to space out further
Requires each follow-up to carry a genuinely new angle - a stat, a case study, an insight - rather than a reminder
Caps the follow-up count at three for the default sponsorship cadence
Spaces pings one to two weeks apart and identifies the day-4 ping as too tight at five months out
States the 3-4 day tightening applies only close to the event date, not five months out
Ties the final reminder to a real, verifiable production date already on the calendar, such as a merchandise print cutoff or a program-lock date, rather than an invented close date
Explains that a deadline the sponsor can verify carries more weight than a stated close date with nothing behind it
Removes the opted-out contact from the sequence immediately, mid-sequence, not at the next scheduled touch
States that the three already-queued sends to that contact must be cancelled now
Warns that following up past the cap costs more goodwill than it recovers
Names the community-reputation cost - burning the event's name among people who talk to each other - as the sponsorship-specific reason for the cap, distinct from any sales-benchmark reasoning

evals.prompt: Our conference wrapped on 6 June. Of last year's ten sponsors, six still have not signed for next year's edition, which lands on 4 June. It is now mid-September and I am finally getting to them. Plan was to run them through the same sequence as our cold list: intro email explaining what the conference is, then the prospectus, then follow-ups. Six of them also ended up on my net-new spreadsheet by accident, which honestly seems fine, one list is simpler to manage.
evals.expected_output: A separate renewal motion that starts near the exploratory-call step, anchored on last edition's post-event sponsor report, with the cold intro email rejected outright, the mid-September start flagged as three months late against a renewal clock that runs from event close, and the merged spreadsheet split back into two tracked motions with their own conversion rates.
expectations: Rejects running the six returning sponsors through the net-new sequence
States that an email explaining what the event is, sent to a company that wrote a check for it last year, reads as not knowing your own sponsors
States that renewal outreach starts at or within days of event close, not months later
Identifies mid-September, roughly three months after the 6 June close, as late on the renewal clock and notes the sponsor's attention or budget line has had time to move elsewhere
Anchors the renewal conversation on last edition's post-event sponsor report
Notes that renewal outreach without that report is just a cold email to someone who happens to know you
Enters the renewal sequence at or near the exploratory-call step, skipping the research step and the cold first touch
Rejects merging renewal and net-new into one list and requires the two motions be tracked separately
Requires separate stage-conversion rates for the renewal motion and the net-new motion
Keeps the eight-months-out fiscal-year checkpoint on the net-new track only, rather than applying it to renewals
Notes that renewal conversion also reads as a demand signal about the event itself, not only as a measure of outreach quality

evals.prompt: Call tomorrow with Vantage Cloud, who would be our biggest backer yet at EUR 15,000 for SaltMarsh Conf. We are community-run, all volunteers, 600 people. Their marketing director already emailed three asks: a 30-minute keynote slot for their CTO, badge scanning at their booth, and the attendee list as a CSV afterwards. She also wrote 'honestly we sponsored a conference two years ago and got nothing out of it'. How do I handle all this on the call? Give me something I can keep open on a second screen while we talk.
evals.expected_output: A quick-reference table usable mid-call, with each objection carried through the objection statement, the real concern beneath it, a response approach, a proof point and a follow-up question. The keynote slot, badge scanning and attendee-list asks are all refused for a community-run event with substitutes offered, the 'got nothing out of it' objection is turned into a metric-setting conversation, and the EUR 15,000 top-tier size triggers a values-alignment check inside the organizing team.
expectations: Refuses to sell the 30-minute keynote slot at a community-run event and points to the CFP or an open-space / topic-suggestion path instead
Refuses to hand over the attendee list as a CSV and offers aggregate audience composition instead
Refuses badge scanning as a community-run deliverable and offers conversation-based formats plus aggregate demographics in its place
Handles the 'we got nothing out of it' objection by first asking which success metric they used on that past sponsorship
Proposes agreeing one measurable goal for this sponsorship before anything is signed
Points to the post-event sponsor report as the proof point for that objection
Delivers the answers as a quick-reference table scannable mid-call, matching the second-screen request
Structures each objection with the statement as actually said, the real concern beneath it, a response approach, a proof point and a follow-up question
Flags that at EUR 15,000, the largest pledge the event has taken, a values-alignment check inside the organizing team is warranted before the deal is finalized
Tags each objection heard with the sponsor's segment and logs it, rather than answering and moving on
Has the fixed operational checklist answered before the call - projected attendance, aggregate audience composition, per-level benefits, and logistics such as power, network, table size and shipping

evals.prompt: First edition of Tuulikko, a Rust systems conference in Tampere, 250 people, next May. Zero sponsor history, and none of the four organizers works anywhere that would plausibly write us a check. A friend has offered us his ZoomInfo export for free: roughly 4,000 DevRel and marketing contacts at infrastructure vendors, already filtered to Nordics. Where do we actually get sponsors from, and is the export worth using?
evals.expected_output: The purchased export ruled out entirely rather than kept as a fallback, on compliance grounds, plus a first-edition re-ranked source menu: the missing previous-sponsor roster acknowledged, a franchise or sibling-edition roster asked about, adjacent-event sponsor scanning and attendee-stack vendor mapping promoted with their promotion conditions named, cold email promoted because no organizer network exists, inbound broadcast kept on as background, and every candidate scored with a sourced claim.
expectations: Rules out the ZoomInfo export entirely rather than keeping it as a last resort at the bottom of the channel menu
States that contacts must come from public business channels only, with no scraped or purchased lists
Frames that exclusion as a compliance matter covering consent and e-marketing law, not merely a quality preference
Notes that a first edition has no previous-sponsor roster, so the default first source is unavailable
Asks whether the event belongs to a franchise or multi-city series whose sibling or local editions' sponsor roster could substitute

Names the adjacent-event sponsor scan - companies publicly listed as sponsors of neighbouring events in the same technology space - and explains that published sponsor pages are public evidence of budget, motivation and fit

Names attendee-stack vendor mapping - identifying which vendors' tools the expected audience uses or evaluates, then targeting those vendors' DevRel and marketing teams - and identifies it as the highest-research-effort source
Justifies promoting that high-effort source here on the grounds that the warm lists are absent or exhausted against the revenue goal
Promotes the cold email sequence explicitly because a first edition with no organizer network has no warm paths left to exhaust
Keeps an inbound broadcast - a sponsorship-call post on the event's own site plus social posts - running as background while stating it must not be the plan
Scores each candidate Hot / Warm / Cold / Skip with a source URL and date attached to each qualification claim

evals.prompt: Good news, Halden Robotics just said yes on the phone to EUR 6,000 for Lumen Devcon. Payment terms are whatever, we will sort that out closer to the date. Our treasurer opened a new bank account for the association last month and I am fairly sure the IBAN works. What do I do now before I go back to working the rest of the list?
evals.expected_output: Immediate invoicing, a written confirmation of amount and payment method replacing 'we will sort it out', verification that the new receiving account and currency actually work before payment is sent, a handoff to the agreement step, a named liaison who owns the relationship through fulfillment, the pipeline record advanced, and the sponsor's budget-cycle month captured for next edition.
expectations: Invoices immediately rather than waiting until closer to the event date
Produces a written confirmation of the amount and the payment method, rejecting leaving terms as something to sort out later
Verifies that the newly opened receiving account and its currency actually work for the organizing entity before payment is sent, rather than assuming the IBAN is fine
Hands the deal to the sponsorship agreement and contracting step for terms
Names one dedicated liaison, a specific organizer, who owns contact, payment chasing and discount codes for Halden Robotics
States that the liaison assignment persists through fulfillment rather than ending at signature
Advances Halden Robotics to the committed or signed stage in the pipeline rather than leaving the record at proposal sent
Gates the closing step by deal size, not only by the deliverables the pledge buys
Records the sponsor's budget-cycle month alongside the liaison and pipeline record, so next edition's outreach starts from it
